entry.title: Learning Lattice Parameters from Powder X-Ray Diffraction Data Using Invariants

link.title: Learning Lattice Parameters from Powder X-Ray Diffraction Data Using Invariants

entry.content:
Introduction

Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) is a core tool for characterizing materials. In general, traditional methods extract peak positions and then assess trial unit cells in order to determine the correct lattice parameters, a process known as indexing. This can be difficult in the presence of severe peak overlap, for low-symmetry crystals, or for materials with a large unit cell axis (dominant zones). Discriminating between competing solutions can become an art form relying on the prior knowledge of the crystallographer. There has been growing interest in using machine learning (ML) to narrow this search.

Recent work trains neural networks to predict the six lattice parameters \((a, b, c, \alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) directly from a powder pattern . However, these lattice parameters are not an ideal target for an ML model, as they depend on the choice of unit cell and can change discontinuously near symmetry boundaries. We instead predict the lattice bispectrum, a smooth descriptor that is invariant to the choice of cell, and recover the lattice parameters by inverting it. With the same architecture, this reduces length error on MP-20 from 11.1% to 2.4% and angle error from 12.2% to 2.5%.

Unit Cell Representations

A lattice can be generated by three vectors, whose lengths and relative angles give the lattice parameters. However, infinitely many sets of vectors generate the same lattice. Unit cell reduction procedures select a canonical set, but they are defined piecewise across crystal systems. Small continuous changes in a lattice can therefore produce discontinuous jumps in the lattice parameters near symmetry boundaries, even though the underlying geometry changes smoothly. This has practical consequences for ML, as the lattice parameters are a discontinuous learning target. A model predicting lattice parameters must implicitly learn a single consistent convention.

Interpolation between a cubic and a triclinic lattice. The bispectrum (top row) varies smoothly along this path, while the reduced-cell distance \(S^6\) (bottom left) is non-smooth because of changes in the chosen reduced basis.

In dominant zone structures, usually those with one axis much longer than the others, most reflections can be indexed with only two Miller indices. The diffraction pattern then leaves the remaining lattice geometry underconstrained, which is difficult for both traditional indexing algorithms and neural networks.

Lattice Bispectrum

A useful lattice descriptor should be independent of primitive cell choice, continuous under smooth lattice deformations, and expressed in reciprocal space, where diffraction operates. Our workflow predicts such a descriptor from the XRD pattern, inverts it to obtain a set of lattice vectors, and then converts these vectors to standard lattice parameters.

Workflow for predicting the bispectrum and inverting it to obtain lattice parameters.

Given reciprocal lattice vectors \(\{\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \mathbf{b}_3\}\), each reciprocal lattice point is \(\mathbf{G} = h\mathbf{b}_1 + k\mathbf{b}_2 + l\mathbf{b}_3\) with \(h, k, l \in \mathbb{Z}\). We take all points within a cutoff \(k_{\max}\), which corresponds to the limiting resolution of the detector, and write the lattice as

\[\rho(\mathbf{k}) = \sum_{|\mathbf{G}| \leq k_{\max}} \delta(\mathbf{k} - \mathbf{G})\]

We then expand \(\rho\) using spherical harmonics \(Y_{lm}\) for the angular part and radial basis functions \(g_n\) for the radial part, which gives the coefficients

\[c_{nlm} = \sum_{|\mathbf{G}| \leq k_{\max}} Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf{G}})\, g_n(|\mathbf{G}|)\]

Invariant descriptors can be obtained from successive tensor products of these coefficients. The simplest is the power spectrum, \(\sum_m \lvert c_{nlm} \rvert^2\), but this loses information about correlations between different \(l\) channels. To retain more information, we couple coefficients from three channels \((l_1, l_2, l_3)\) into scalars through a symmetrized Clebsch-Gordan tensor product, following the standard construction from the atomistic ML literature :

\[\mathbf{B} = \big(\mathbf{c}_{l_3} \otimes (\mathbf{c}_{l_1} \otimes \mathbf{c}_{l_2})\big)^{(0_e \oplus 0_o)}\]

where \((0_e \oplus 0_o)\) indicates that we keep scalars and pseudoscalars. All pseudoscalars vanish for Bravais lattices since they are centrosymmetric, but we retain these channels for generality. In this work, we use \(l_{\max} = 6\) and 10 Bessel radial basis functions, with \(k_{\max} \approx 2/3\) Å⁻¹. Each row of the resulting descriptor corresponds to a radial basis function and each column to an allowed coupling, so the bispectrum can be visualized as a 2D heatmap.

This construction has the following properties:

  • Independent of primitive cell choice: Any set of primitive vectors generates the same lattice points, and \(c_{nlm}\) is a sum over these points.
  • Invariant under \(O(3)\): The construction is rotationally invariant, and every reciprocal lattice is centrosymmetric. This is consistent with powder diffraction, which is insensitive to orientation and measures the same intensity at \(\mathbf{G}\) and \(-\mathbf{G}\).
  • Smooth: The bispectrum varies smoothly in \(L^2\) norm under continuous lattice deformations.
  • Reflects lattice symmetry: Only certain \((l, m)\) channels can be non-zero for a given point group, so higher-symmetry lattices produce more zero entries. For example, only \(l = 0, 4, 6, 8, \ldots\) contribute for a cubic lattice.
Sample bispectra for lattices with varying levels of symmetry. The sparsity pattern reflects the symmetry of the lattice, with higher-symmetry lattices producing more zero entries.

Inverting the Bispectrum

The bispectrum is not guaranteed to be a one-to-one mapping, but it can be inverted empirically . Since the computation of \(\mathbf{B}\) is differentiable in PyTorch, we can use L-BFGS-B to optimize a lattice until its bispectrum matches the target. To initialize the optimization, we retrieve the 15 nearest entries from a precomputed database of Materials Project bispectra and use these as starting points, stopping once a candidate reaches a sufficiently low bispectrum loss. The inversion yields a set of vectors spanning the lattice, which we convert to conventional lattice parameters using pymatgen or cctbx.

Predicting the Bispectrum from XRD

We use a transformer to predict the bispectrum from the XRD pattern. Previous works have used convolutional neural networks (CNNs), but these are translation invariant and cannot directly relate peaks across the full pattern. Self-attention allows every peak to attend to every other peak, and preserves absolute peak positions. To evaluate the effect of the representation, we train the same architecture to output either the lattice parameters or the bispectrum, changing only the output dimension. Both the true and predicted lattices are passed through cctbx before computing errors, so that all comparisons are made in a consistent setting.

Results

Simulated Patterns

We train on four sets of simulated patterns: MP-20 (Materials Project structures with up to 20 atoms per unit cell , 27K patterns), the full Materials Project (93K patterns), and augmented versions of each (270K and 930K patterns). The physics-based augmentations include strain, peak intensity and width variation, and background noise. Predicting the bispectrum reduces length, angle, and volume MAPE by a factor of 1.8 to 5 on every dataset.

Mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) for direct prediction and bispectrum + inversion using the same transformer. MP-20 models are evaluated on the MP-20 test set and MP-Full models on the MP-Full test set.

This improvement is likely due in part to the bispectrum preserving lattice symmetry. Without separate models for each crystal system, direct prediction may yield values that do not align with the correct Bravais lattice, such as cubic angles that are not exactly 90°. The bispectrum does not show this behavior, as it already encodes the symmetry of the lattice.

Dominant Zones

We define dominant zone patterns as those with at least 50% of their total intensity in a single zero-index family of reflections (\(h = 0\), \(k = 0\), or \(l = 0\)), which applies to 1,100 of the 30,000 structures in the full Materials Project test set. Using the model trained on the augmented full Materials Project, 76.6% of bispectrum predictions on these structures have both length and angle MAPE below 5%, compared to 5.8% of direct predictions. Direct prediction also often mispredicts symmetry-fixed angles of 90° and 120°, whereas bispectrum inversion largely preserves them.

Parity plots for dominant zone structures, for bispectrum inversion (left) and direct prediction (right). Top: predicted vs. true longest axis. Bottom: predicted vs. true lattice angles. The columns at 90° and 120° are angles fixed by symmetry.

Experimental Data

We first evaluate on the 134 experimental RRUFF patterns used to evaluate Crystalyze , a generative model that predicts full crystal structures. Although our model predicts only the lattice, the bispectrum approach achieves performance comparable to Crystalyze:

Method (trained on MP-20 Aug) Length MAE (Å) Length MAPE (%) Angle MAPE (%) Volume MAPE (%)
Bispectrum + inversion (ours) 0.91 14.4 8.9 35.7
Crystalyze 0.90 16.1 9.9 43.4
Direct prediction (ours) 1.86 30.9 10.3 94.8

On the 240 RRUFF patterns used to evaluate AlphaDiffract , our model underperforms AlphaDiffract, particularly for angles. This is expected given that AlphaDiffract trains on 31 million patterns, about 33 times the size of our training set. Our length MAE is nonetheless relatively close (2.50 vs. 2.11 Å). Scaling our model by 1.5x and 2x gave only small improvements, which suggests that model capacity is not the primary bottleneck.

We also evaluate on single-phase CNRS patterns from the opXRD database , where both models show larger errors than on RRUFF. With our original training setup, direct prediction outperforms the bispectrum model on these patterns (length MAPE of 39.2% vs. 43.4%, angle MAPE of 8.9% vs. 15.0%). Since our background noise augmentation was fit to RRUFF, we hypothesize that this is due to a mismatch in noise. Retraining with CNRS-informed noise reduces the bispectrum length MAPE to 26.6%, and using peak lists as input reduces it further to 17.3%. With CNRS-informed noise, 25% of bispectrum predictions have both length and angle MAPE below 5%, whereas fewer than 5% of direct predictions reach this on any experimental dataset. This suggests that noise augmentation fit to one experimental dataset may not generalize to others.

Limitations and Future Work

There are several limitations to our approach:

  • Inversion cost: Inversion takes a median of 88 seconds per structure on a single CPU core with 15 starting candidates. This is parallelizable, but much slower than a forward pass of the model.
  • Out-of-distribution patterns: For experimental patterns far from the training data, bispectrum predictions are further from the ground truth. This makes inversion more difficult and can degrade the predicted lattice parameters.
  • Simulation to real gap: Performance on experimental data remains below performance on simulated data. Closing this gap will likely require larger datasets and augmentations that better capture experimental artifacts.
  • Lack of a standard benchmark: Different works use different training data, splits, and augmentations. A shared benchmark with a fixed training set, augmentation protocol, and test split would allow direct comparison between methods, and would ideally include experimental data currently scattered across personal repositories.

The lattice bispectrum could also be useful for other crystallographic ML tasks. For example, structure generation models could condition on the bispectrum rather than on raw lattice parameters. Since determining a lattice from an XRD pattern is fundamentally a one-to-many problem, a generative version of our approach that samples candidate lattices would be a natural extension. Incorporating the structure factor could also yield a descriptor sensitive to both the lattice and the atomic basis, which could aid in full structure determination.

Conclusion

We introduce an invariant, invertible representation of the reciprocal lattice and show that using it as the prediction target improves lattice parameter prediction from powder XRD. While ML for science often focuses on inputs and architectures, these results suggest that the choice of target deserves more attention, particularly when the standard representation is ambiguous or discontinuous.

Read More

  • Paper: Learning lattice parameters from powder X-ray diffraction data using invariants, Acta Cryst. A (2027), doi:10.1107/S2053273326010284
  • arXiv: arxiv.org/abs/2607.21829
  • Code, dataset splits and precomputed bispectra: github.com/atomicarchitects/bispectrum-xrd-ml

We thank Nina Andrejevic for helpful information about AlphaDiffract, Eric Riesel for discussions regarding Crystalyze, and Emily Oliphant and Ameya Daigavane for helpful discussions regarding our methodology.
entry.summary: Machine learning models have been used to aid in predicting lattice parameters from powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) data. The lattice parameters of a crystal are subject to conventions (e.g., primitive vs. conventional cells) and can change discontinuously at symmetry boundaries between Bravais lattices. We present an invariant representation of the reciprocal lattice, based on spherical harmonic projections, that is independent of cell convention, differentiable, and invertible. When predicting unit cells from powder X-ray diffraction data, replacing lattice parameters with this representation as the learning target reduces errors by a up to a factor of five.

entry.title: To Augment or Not to Augment? Diagnosing Distributional Symmetry Breaking

link.title: To Augment or Not to Augment? Diagnosing Distributional Symmetry Breaking

entry.content:
Introduction

For a group transformation \(g \in G\) (e.g. a rotation or permutation), a model is equivariant if \(f(gx) = g f(x)\) — rotating the input rotates the output — and invariant if \(f(gx) = f(x)\) — the output is unchanged. Equivariant architectures enforce this by design; data augmentation encourages it by randomly applying \(g\) to training inputs. Equivariant models have had successes in multiple domanains - materials science , robotics , drug discovery , fluid dynamics , computer vision , and beyond.

Both approaches rely on the assumption that the ground truth function \(f\) is equivariant. However, there is often an implicit assumption that the data distribution itself is symmetric, i.e. \(p(x) \approx p(gx)\). We refer to violations of this assumption as distributional symmetry breaking. In this work, we study distributional symmetry breaking. Our main contributions are:

  • A classifier-based diagnostic: We introduce a simple two-sample test to measure distributional symmetry breaking.

  • Theoretical analysis: We show that data augmentation can harm performance under certain distributional conditions.

  • Empirical studies: We demonstrate that widely used 3D datasets are strongly canonicalized. We correspondingly evaluate the impacts of equivariant methods on datasets across domains and propose hypotheses for differing behaviors.

Distributional Symmetry Breaking

Examples of distributional symmetry breaking. Left: Baseballs appear in all orientations equally — the distribution is symmetric. Middle-left: Coffee mugs have a preferred orientation (handle to the side), illustrating a mild symmetry bias. Middle-right: Canonicalization maps arbitrary orientations to a single canonical one — the strongest form of symmetry breaking. Right: Inherent canonicalization (digits 6/9) and user-defined canonicalization (crystal lattice), where orientation is either intrinsically meaningful or fixed by convention.

Distributional symmetry breaking may lead equivariant methods or data augmentation to discard useful information. For example, classifying 6s and 9s in MNIST is easy when the digits appear in their natural orientation, but it becomes harder under rotational augmentation.

Proposed Metric

The goal: define a metric \(m(p_X)\) that quantifies how far a data distribution \(p_X\) is from being group-symmetric — without assuming symmetry in the first place.

The key reference is the symmetrized density \(\bar{p}_X(x) := \int_{g \in G} p_X(gx)\, dg\), the closest group-invariant distribution to \(p_X\). Measuring \(m(p_X)\) reduces to measuring how distinguishable \(p_X\) and \(\bar{p}_X\) are from finite samples.

Why not MMD? A natural approach is Maximum Mean Discrepancy with a chosen kernel. But there is no universal kernel — for geometric graph datasets like molecular structures, choosing a kernel that captures chemical information is non-trivial, and the resulting values are not directly interpretable.

Our approach: a two-sample classifier test. We train a small neural network to distinguish samples from \(p_X\) (original) versus \(\bar{p}_X\) (randomly transformed), and use test accuracy as the metric:

\[m(p_X) := \mathbb{E}_{(x,c) \in D^*_{\text{test}}} \left[ \mathbf{1}\big(\text{NN}(x) = c\big) \right]\]

Algorithm:

  1. Split the dataset in half.
  2. Apply random \(g \sim G\) to one half — these approximate \(\bar{p}_X\) (label 1).
  3. Keep the other half unchanged as \(p_X\) (label 0).
  4. Train a binary classifier and report test accuracy as \(m(p_X)\).

Interpretation:

  • \(m(p_X) \approx 0.5\): data is (approximately) group-invariant — the classifier can’t do better than chance.
  • \(m(p_X) \approx 1\): data is strongly canonicalized — the classifier easily detects the preferred orientations.

Task-Dependent Metric

\(m(p_X)\) tells us whether the data breaks symmetry — but not whether that matters for the specific task. Consider MNIST digits 6 and 9: they are canonicalized in a way that is directly predictive of the label. Augmenting away orientation destroys this useful signal.

We introduce \(t(p_{X,Y})\), a metric of task-useful distributional symmetry breaking. Let \(c\colon\mathcal{X} \rightarrow G\) be a canonicalization function (implemented as a randomly initialized, untrained equivariant network). Since data augmentation destroys information in \(c(x)\), we ask: how much does \(c(x)\) predict the label \(f(x)\)?

We compare:

  • \(\mathcal{L}(c(x) \to f(x))\): loss when predicting labels from orientations (canonical orientation intact)
  • \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{rot}} = \mathcal{L}(c(gx) \to f(gx),\, g \sim G)\): same, but with random rotations applied — removing orientation information
\[t(p_{X,Y}) := \frac{\mathcal{L}_{\text{rot}}}{\mathcal{L}}\]
  • \(t \gg 1\): orientations carry task-relevant signal — augmentation likely hurts by discarding it.
  • \(t \approx 1\): orientation is not predictive — augmentation is likely safe or beneficial.

Theory

To understand when augmentation can backfire, we analyze a tractable setting: high-dimensional ridge regression where the true function is invariant, but the data distribution may not be. Our theory shows that even when the ground-truth function is invariant, data augmentation and test-time symmetrization can be harmful when invariant and non-invariant features are strongly correlated.

Takeaway: Symmetry enforcement can hurt by discarding signal that, while technically non-invariant, is informative about the label via its correlation with invariant features.

Summary of theoretical results. Rows: weak vs. strong correlation between invariant and non-invariant features. Columns: under- vs. over-parameterized regime. Augmentation can hurt in the over-parameterized + strong correlation setting, where non-invariant features act as proxies for invariant ones.
Left three panels: Excess risk, bias, and variance of vanilla (blue) vs. augmented (orange) models as feature correlation strength \(\sigma_w\) varies. At low \(\sigma_w\) (strongly correlated features, high symmetry breaking), augmentation increases excess risk — driven by higher variance. Right: Corresponding \(m(p_X)\) values, which are highest at low \(\sigma_w\), confirming the metric tracks symmetry breaking accurately.

We thus find invariance interacts with data geometry and high-dimensional statistics in subtle ways. When the data distribution breaks symmetry — even slightly — enforcing invariance can destroy useful signal. And in modern over-parameterized regimes, reducing effective dimension can itself introduce instability.

Invariance is not just a property of the target function — it’s also a property of the data distribution. If those two don’t align, enforcing symmetry can hurt.

This raises a puzzle: if datasets like QM9 are strongly canonicalized, our theory predicts augmentation should hurt — yet empirically it helps. We investigate this discrepancy below.

Experiments

How canonicalized are real datasets?

We measure \(m(p_X)\) on multiple benchmark datasets. Strikingly, many widely-used benchmarks are strongly canonicalized — particularly molecular and materials science datasets — even though equivariant methods are routinely applied to them under the assumption of distributional symmetry.

Takeaway: Real-world datasets often deviate substantially from the symmetry assumptions built into equivariant models.

Does canonicalization predict whether augmentation helps?

We evaluate equivariant, group-averaged, and stochastic group-averaged models on each dataset. The results are summarized below.

Comparison of train/test augmentation, group-averaged, and equivariant models across datasets. Augmentation: TT = train+test, TF = train only, FT = test only, FF = none. MNIST uses a group-averaged model; other datasets use stochastic group-averaging. MAE is reported for QM7b/QM9; equivariant baselines from e3nn. Best overall in bold, best within augmentation underlined. CNN used for MNIST, graph transformer for point clouds.
Dataset Symmetry \(m(p_X)\) Effect of Augmentation / Equivariance
MNIST \(C_4\) rotations High Minimal benefit; slight harm
ModelNet40 SO(3) rotations High (class-specific) Reduces performance
QM9 SO(3) rotations High (CORINA preprocessing ) Improves nearly all properties
QM7b SO(3) rotations High Beneficial, especially for non-scalar properties (e.g. dipole)

While one might expect augmentation to consistently hurt on canonicalized datasets, molecular datasets (QM7b and QM9) defy this picture.

Takeaway: Whether symmetry methods help or hurt is dataset-dependent — canonicalization alone does not predict the outcome.

Additional Materials Science Datasets

We extend the analysis to additional materials science datasets:

  • rMD17 : Molecular dynamics trajectories for small molecules. The degree of distributional symmetry breaking varies widely between molecules — reflecting differences in initial conditions and molecular geometry.
  • OC20 : Adsorbates on periodic crystalline catalysts. Both the adsorbate alone and the adsorbate+catalyst system are highly canonicalized, likely due to the catalyst surface being aligned with the \(xy\) plane.
  • LLM crystal dataset : Crystals serialized to text for LLM generation. Atoms must be listed in some order — the authors independently noted that permutation augmentations hurt generative performance. We trained a classifier head on a pretrained DistilBERT transformer to test this, and found \(m(p_X) = 95\%\) — strong permutation canonicalization due to conventions in atom ordering.

Takeaway: Distributional symmetry breaking is widespread across data types and modalities — not just 3D point clouds.

Hypotheses for Empirical Behavior

We present hypotheses for the differing performance of equivariant models/data augmentation across datasets.

Task Dependent Metric

We apply \(t(p_{X,Y})\) to each dataset to ask: does the canonical orientation actually carry task-relevant information?

  • QM7b dipole (artificial canonicalization): Molecules are aligned so their dipole moments point along the \(z\) axis — orientation is directly predictive of the label. A non-equivariant model can exploit this; an equivariant one cannot. As expected: no-augmentation (FF) outperforms the equivariant baseline, and \(t \gg 1\).

  • ModelNet40: Same story — equivariance hurts and \(t\) is large. Object identity is correlated with how the object is canonically oriented.

  • QM9: \(t \approx 1\) — canonical orientation carries little task-relevant information globally. Equivariance does destroy orientation, but since that orientation wasn’t predictive to begin with, nothing useful is lost. This is consistent with equivariance helping.

Task-dependent metric \(t(p_{X,Y})\): Accuracy (ModelNet) or MAE (QM7b/QM9) when predicting labels from the canonicalization vs. a random-rotation baseline. Values averaged over five seeds. Higher ratio = more task-relevant signal in the orientation.

Takeaway: \(t\) is large for datasets where equivariance hurts, and small where it helps — it tells us whether augmentation discards task-relevant signal.

But \(t\) only explains why equivariance doesn’t hurt on QM9 — not why it actively improves performance. For that, we need to look at local structure.

Locality

Equivariant models compute locally equivariant features over receptive fields — their benefit may come from capturing symmetry in small recurring motifs rather than enforcing global symmetry . We test this by applying \(m(p_X)\) at both global and local scales.

  • QM9: Local bond neighborhoods have much lower \(m(p_X)\) than the full molecule — local structure is close to isotropic even when the global dataset is canonicalized. Equivariant models can exploit this local symmetry.
  • ModelNet40: Local neighborhoods also show lower \(m(p_X)\) at small sizes, but canonical alignment re-emerges as neighborhoods grow — the canonical orientation is object-level and tightly coupled to the task.
Left: Local QM9 neighborhoods and their \(m(p_X)\) values. Right: Local ModelNet40 results as neighborhood size grows.
The relevant question is not simply whether a dataset is canonicalized, but at what scale canonicalization interacts with the task.

Based on these findings, we provide the following flowchart as a practical guide for deciding whether to use equivariant methods or data augmentation on a new dataset:

Advice for practitioners on using our metric for model selection.

Conclusion

We provide interpretable metrics for diagnosing distributional symmetry breaking — no domain knowledge required. Every benchmark dataset we tested showed a high degree of symmetry-breaking, yet augmentation only hurt performance on ModelNet40.

Three implications stand out. First, non-equivariant models evaluated only on in-distribution data may appear accurate but fail under transformations — assessing whether this matters requires domain expertise (see the flowchart above). Second, data augmentation is often treated as universally beneficial for invariant tasks, but we show it can hurt. Third, if already-canonicalized molecular datasets still benefit from equivariance, equivariant models must provide some additional, possibly domain-specific benefit beyond global symmetry enforcement — a compelling open question.
entry.summary: Many popular ML datasets are heavily canonicalized — objects almost always appear in the same orientation. We measure this with a simple classifier test, showing theoretically that canonicalization can cause data augmentation to hurt performance. We give practitioners a flowchart for diagnosing their own datasets.
